title: Air India Plans September Flight Comeback With More Frequencies to New York, Tokyo and Milan
excerpt: The Tata-owned carrier will restore most curtailed international routes from September 1, adding services to key destinations as fleet availability improves.
body:
• Air India will restore most curtailed international flights from September 1, ending a three-month network rationalisation.
  • Additional frequencies will be added on routes to Milan, Frankfurt, Zurich, Melbourne, Tokyo and New York.
  • Services to Chicago O'Hare and Washington Dulles remain suspended due to limited aircraft availability.
  • Deliveries of new Airbus A350-1000 aircraft are expected toward the end of 2026, boosting long-haul capacity.

Air India will restore the bulk of its curtailed international flights from September 1, the carrier confirmed on Thursday, marking the end of a three-month network rationalisation triggered by operational disruptions and a sharp rise in fuel prices.

Route Restoration and New Frequencies

The airline is adding frequencies on several high-demand international routes. Additional services will go to Milan, Frankfurt and Zurich in Europe, while Melbourne, Tokyo and New York will also see restored or increased flight counts, according to The Economic Times.

Delhi to Zurich will see full restoration with frequency even being added beyond pre-cut levels. Tokyo and Seoul routes from Delhi will also return to their full schedules. The carrier's European operations are expected to normalise from September as frequencies are progressively restored during August, with Newark Liberty among the US destinations regaining additional services.

"The temporary reductions were always planned as a short-term measure, with services from September onward never removed from our reservation system."

— Air India spokesperson

Routes Still Suspended

Not all routes will return immediately. Services to Chicago O'Hare and Washington Dulles will remain suspended for the time being. The continued absence of these routes is attributed to aircraft shortages caused by an ongoing fleet retrofit programme, delays in new aircraft deliveries and the retirement of older Boeing 777-200LR aircraft, according to Aviation A2Z.

The Ahmedabad to London route, which was altered following the Air India 171 crash, will resume with reduced frequency — three times weekly instead of the original five — and will operate into London Heathrow rather than Gatwick.

Fleet Modernisation Drives Expansion

Air India's network rebuild is underpinned by its Vihaan.AI transformation programme, which includes orders for 570 new jets from Airbus and Boeing. Deliveries of the Airbus A350-1000, the carrier's next-generation long-haul workhorse, are expected to begin toward the end of 2026.

The airline has already begun deploying retrofitted aircraft with new cabin products on several routes. More than half of flights to North America now feature updated interiors, including new business class seats and the rollout of premium economy on additional sectors. A new seasonal Mumbai-Toronto non-stop service is also set to launch on October 25 using the brand-new Boeing 787-9.

What NRIs Should Know

For diaspora travellers, the September restoration means better options on the most popular India-US and India-Europe corridors. The majority of September schedules are already on sale, allowing passengers to book well in advance. However, those relying on the Chicago and Washington routes will need to continue using alternative connections until fleet availability improves.

New CEO Tewolde Gebremariam, the former Ethiopian Airlines chief appointed last week, inherits the challenge of executing this restoration while managing the airline's broader transformation. Air India was operating over 525 weekly international flights to 63 destinations as of mid-June, and the carrier aims to exceed those levels once the full fleet returns to service.
nri_angle: NRI travellers will benefit from restored flight frequencies on key India-US and India-Europe corridors starting September, though Chicago and Washington routes remain suspended.
author: Diaspora Desk
